newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican who led vendors from her taco stand mourned.
newsitem.headline: Mexican who led vendors from her taco stand mourned.

text.p: Grief-stricken street vendors in the Mexican capital on Thursday mourned the death of their long-standing defender who commanded a power base from her taco stand.
Guillermina Rico, who went from selling lemons to leading 12,000 street vendors in one of the world's largest cities, died from a brain haemorrhage on Wednesday at the age of 63.

"We're orphans now," Luis Campa, a street vendor with tears in his eyes told local television. "Our lives depend on God's tender mercy now," he added as vendors paid their respects to the matriarch who led them for forty years.
Just days ago, Rico, known by her nickname "Dona Guille," was still active tending one of her five taco stands in the city centre.
Her death has left vendors wondering who will defend them from frequent attacks by police and officials anxious to drive them away to brush up the image of the city's historic centre.
Steet selling has soared since an economic crisis hit Mexico in December 1994, thowing more than a million people out of work.
Dona Guille was often seen wandering around the crumbling city centre in her hallmark white apron, lending a friendly ear to her followers.

At her command, the vendors would turn into shock troops whenever a police crackdown was threatened. They also paid her hefty dues. Local newspapers calculated that each stall paid her between the equivalent of $600 and $1,200 a year.
The price of protection was also unconditional support for the Revolutionary Institutional Party, which has governed Mexico for 67 years.
A bloc of 12,000 votes delivered every election day often smoothed over relations with the local authorities.
